paragraphs.text: A rolled [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) from 1989, now thirty-seven years old. It is [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), old tea, in the island's sense: oolong kept for years and roasted again at low heat from time to time, to drive out the moisture it takes in while it rests. No standard sets how many years make an oolong old. Those who give a figure put it somewhere between ten and thirty, and this tea has passed the longest of them.

The origin is given only as [Taiwan](taiwan:on-a-label). That places the leaf on the island, whose tea plants and craft came from Fujian, but says nothing of the mountain, the height or the cultivar it grew from.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
